{{Short description|Measurability theorem}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Hahn decomposition theorem''', named after the [[Austria]]n [[mathematician]] [[Hans Hahn (mathematician)|Hans Hahn]], states that for any [[sigma-algebra|measurable space]] <math> (X,\Sigma) </math> and any [[signed measure]] <math> \mu </math> defined on the <math> \sigma </math>-algebra <math> \Sigma </math>, there exist two <math> \Sigma </math>-measurable sets, <math> P </math> and <math> N </math>, of <math> X </math> such that:

# <math> P \cup N = X </math> and  <math> P \cap N = \varnothing </math>.
# For every <math> E \in \Sigma </math> such that <math> E \subseteq P </math>, one has <math> \mu(E) \geq 0 </math>, i.e., <math> P </math> is a [[positive and negative sets|positive set]] for <math> \mu </math>.
# For every <math> E \in \Sigma </math> such that <math> E \subseteq N </math>, one has <math> \mu(E) \leq 0 </math>, i.e., <math> N </math> is a negative set for <math> \mu </math>.

Moreover, this decomposition is [[universal property|essentially unique]], meaning that for any other pair <math> (P',N') </math> of <math> \Sigma </math>-measurable subsets of <math> X </math> fulfilling the three conditions above, the [[symmetric difference]]s <math> P \triangle P' </math> and <math> N \triangle N' </math> are <math> \mu </math>-[[null set]]s in the strong sense that every <math> \Sigma </math>-measurable subset of them has zero measure. The pair <math> (P,N) </math> is then called a ''Hahn decomposition'' of the signed measure <math> \mu </math>.

== Jordan measure decomposition ==

A consequence of the Hahn decomposition theorem is the '''{{visible anchor|Jordan decomposition theorem}}''', which states that every signed measure <math> \mu </math> defined on <math> \Sigma </math> has a ''unique'' decomposition into the difference <math> \mu = \mu^{+} - \mu^{-} </math> of two positive measures, <math> \mu^{+} </math> and <math> \mu^{-} </math>, at least one of which is finite, such that <math> {\mu^{+}}(E) = 0 </math> for every <math> \Sigma </math>-measurable subset <math> E \subseteq N </math> and <math> {\mu^{-}}(E) = 0 </math> for every <math> \Sigma </math>-measurable subset <math> E \subseteq P </math>, for any Hahn decomposition <math> (P,N) </math> of <math> \mu </math>. We call <math> \mu^{+} </math> and <math> \mu^{-} </math> the ''positive'' and ''negative part'' of <math> \mu </math>, respectively. The pair <math> (\mu^{+},\mu^{-}) </math> is called a ''Jordan decomposition'' (or sometimes ''Hahn–Jordan decomposition'') of <math> \mu </math>. The two measures can be defined as

:<math> {\mu^{+}}(E) := \mu(E \cap P) \qquad \text{and} \qquad {\mu^{-}}(E) := - \mu(E \cap N) </math>

for every <math> E \in \Sigma </math> and any Hahn decomposition <math> (P,N) </math> of <math> \mu </math>.

Note that the Jordan decomposition is unique, while the Hahn decomposition is only essentially unique.

The Jordan decomposition has the following corollary: Given a Jordan decomposition <math> (\mu^{+},\mu^{-}) </math> of a finite signed measure <math> \mu </math>, one has

:<math> {\mu^{+}}(E) = \sup_{B \in \Sigma, ~ B \subseteq E} \mu(B) \quad \text{and} \quad {\mu^{-}}(E) = - \inf_{B \in \Sigma, ~ B \subseteq E} \mu(B) </math>

for any <math> E </math> in <math> \Sigma </math>. Furthermore, if <math> \mu = \nu^{+} - \nu^{-} </math> for a pair <math> (\nu^{+},\nu^{-}) </math> of finite non-negative measures on <math> X </math>, then

:<math> \nu^{+} \geq \mu^{+} \quad \text{and} \quad \nu^{-} \geq \mu^{-}. </math>

The last expression means that the Jordan decomposition is the ''minimal'' decomposition of <math> \mu </math> into the difference of non-negative measures. This is the ''minimality property'' of the Jordan decomposition.

'''Proof of the Jordan decomposition:''' For an elementary proof of the existence, uniqueness, and minimality of the Jordan measure decomposition see [https://arxiv.org/abs/1206.5449 Fischer (2012)].

== Proof of the Hahn decomposition theorem ==

'''Preparation:''' Assume that <math> \mu </math> does not take the value <math> - \infty </math> (otherwise decompose according to <math> - \mu </math>). As mentioned above, a negative set is a set <math> A \in \Sigma </math> such that <math> \mu(B) \leq 0 </math> for every <math> \Sigma </math>-measurable subset <math> B \subseteq A </math>.

'''Claim:''' Suppose that <math> D \in \Sigma </math> satisfies <math> \mu(D) \leq 0 </math>. Then there is a negative set <math> A \subseteq D </math> such that <math> \mu(A) \leq \mu(D) </math>.

'''Proof of the claim:''' Define <math> A_{0} := D </math>. [[mathematical induction|Inductively]] assume for <math> n \in \mathbb{N}_{0} </math> that <math> A_{n} \subseteq D </math> has been constructed. Let

:<math> t_{n} := \sup(\{ \mu(B) \mid B \in \Sigma ~ \text{and} ~ B \subseteq A_{n} \}) </math>

denote the [[supremum]] of <math> \mu(B) </math> over all the <math> \Sigma </math>-measurable subsets <math> B </math> of <math> A_{n} </math>. This supremum might ''a priori'' be infinite. As the empty set <math> \varnothing </math> is a possible candidate for <math> B </math> in the definition of <math> t_{n} </math>, and as <math> \mu(\varnothing) = 0 </math>, we have <math> t_{n} \geq 0 </math>. By the definition of <math> t_{n} </math>, there then exists a <math> \Sigma </math>-measurable subset <math> B_{n} \subseteq A_{n} </math> satisfying

:<math> \mu(B_{n}) \geq \min \! \left( 1,\frac{t_{n}}{2} \right). </math>

Set <math> A_{n + 1} := A_{n} \setminus B_{n} </math> to finish the induction step. Finally, define

:<math> A := D \Bigg\backslash \bigcup_{n = 0}^{\infty}  B_{n}. </math>

As the sets <math> (B_{n})_{n = 0}^{\infty} </math> are disjoint subsets of <math> D </math>, it follows from the [[sigma additivity]] of the signed measure <math> \mu </math> that

:<math> \mu(D) = \mu(A) + \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} \mu(B_{n}) \geq \mu(A) + \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} \min \! \left( 1,\frac{t_{n}}{2} \right)\geq \mu(A). </math>

This shows that <math> \mu(A) \leq \mu(D) </math>. Assume <math> A </math> were not a negative set. This means that there would exist a <math> \Sigma </math>-measurable subset <math> B \subseteq A </math> that satisfies <math> \mu(B) > 0 </math>. Then <math> t_{n} \geq \mu(B) </math> for every <math> n \in \mathbb{N}_{0} </math>, so the [[series (mathematics)|series]] on the right would have to diverge to <math> + \infty </math>, implying that <math> \mu(D) = + \infty </math>, which is a contradiction, since <math> \mu(D) \leq 0 </math>. Therefore, <math> A </math> must be a negative set.

'''Construction of the decomposition:''' Set <math> N_{0} = \varnothing </math>. Inductively, given <math> N_{n} </math>, define

:<math> s_{n} := \inf(\{ \mu(D) \mid D \in \Sigma ~ \text{and} ~ D \subseteq X \setminus N_{n} \}). </math>

as the [[infimum]] of <math> \mu(D) </math> over all the <math> \Sigma </math>-measurable subsets <math> D </math> of <math> X \setminus N_{n} </math>. This infimum might ''a priori'' be <math> - \infty </math>. As <math> \varnothing </math> is a possible candidate for <math> D </math> in the definition of <math> s_{n} </math>, and as <math> \mu(\varnothing) = 0 </math>, we have <math> s_{n} \leq 0 </math>. Hence, there exists a <math> \Sigma </math>-measurable subset <math> D_{n} \subseteq X \setminus N_{n} </math> such that

:<math> \mu(D_{n}) \leq \max \! \left( \frac{s_{n}}{2},- 1 \right) \leq 0. </math>

By the claim above, there is a negative set <math> A_{n} \subseteq D_{n} </math> such that <math> \mu(A_{n}) \leq \mu(D_{n}) </math>. Set <math> N_{n + 1} := N_{n} \cup A_{n} </math> to finish the induction step. Finally, define

:<math> N := \bigcup_{n = 0}^{\infty} A_{n}. </math>

As the sets <math> (A_{n})_{n = 0}^{\infty} </math> are disjoint, we have for every <math> \Sigma </math>-measurable subset <math> B \subseteq N </math> that

:<math> \mu(B) = \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} \mu(B \cap A_{n}) </math>

by the sigma additivity of <math> \mu </math>. In particular, this shows that <math> N </math> is a negative set. Next, define <math> P := X \setminus N </math>. If <math> P </math> were not a positive set, there would exist a <math> \Sigma </math>-measurable subset <math> D \subseteq P </math> with <math> \mu(D) < 0 </math>. Then <math> s_{n} \leq \mu(D) </math> for all <math> n \in \mathbb{N}_{0} </math> and{{clarify|reason=see talk page|date=July 2023}}

:<math> \mu(N) = \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} \mu(A_{n}) \leq \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} \max \! \left( \frac{s_{n}}{2},- 1 \right) = - \infty, </math>

which is not allowed for <math> \mu </math>. Therefore, <math> P </math> is a positive set.

'''Proof of the uniqueness statement:'''
Suppose that <math> (N',P') </math> is another Hahn decomposition of <math> X </math>. Then <math> P \cap N' </math>  is a positive set and also a negative set. Therefore, every measurable subset of it has measure zero. The same applies to <math> N \cap P' </math>. As

:<math> P \triangle P' = N \triangle N' = (P \cap N') \cup (N \cap P'), </math>

this completes the proof. [[Q.E.D.]]
